Some came from a spec sheet, some was estimated by someone who knows the process, and some is simulated because the sensor does not exist yet. That blend is normal and fine. The problem is when the twin does not say which part is which.

A twin that hides its provenance fails in a predictable way. Someone notices one number is made up, and from then on nobody trusts any of the numbers, including the ones that were measured carefully. The twin goes from decision tool to demo in a single meeting.

Five labels are enough

Across my recent builds I have used the same five labels:

LabelMeaningExample
CapturedMeasured from the real thingGaussian splats trained from video of a racking aisle
DesignedDrawn or modeled for the twinA Blender model of the parts of the building no camera saw
PublishedTaken from a public, citable sourceA kitchen's floor area and equipment schedule, from published sources
EstimatedA judgment call by someone who knows the processOperation times not stated in any recipe
SimulatedGenerated by a model, because no sensor exists yetFreezer temperatures and forklift positions

Five is a small enough set that people remember it, and it covers every case I have met.

Put the label on the record, not in a footnote

A provenance note on a slide gets lost the first time someone screenshots a chart. The label has to travel with the data.

In the Michelin Kitchen Twin, every record in the master data has a src list pointing at a bibliography, or est: true. A validator fails the build if a reference is broken. In the Food Bank Spatial Twin, every API payload carries simulated: true, so no dashboard, script or person downstream can mistake the feed for a real sensor. In the Academic Matchmaker, records missing a verified email or an institutional page carry flags like missing_email and are sorted after fully verified ones.

The same idea shows up in the UI. In the food bank twin's architecture diagrams, solid boxes are deployed and dashed boxes are designed and priced but not built. The browser badge says "Simulated feed" until the live API answers, then "Live from AWS". The labels cost almost nothing to add, and they answer the first question every serious reviewer asks.

Labels make the real parts more valuable

The counterintuitive effect is that labeling the estimated parts makes the measured parts more credible. When a reader can see that the freezer temperatures are simulated, they can trust that the splat capture of the aisle really came from the video. When the kitchen's recipe quantities for one dish are marked as published and tested against the source, the estimated timings next to them read as honest estimates rather than hidden guesses.

Labels also tell you where to spend money next. In the food bank twin, the labels made the next step obvious. The geometry is good enough to start. The simulated telemetry is the gap, and real sensors are priced at about $2,700 once and $12 a month. Without labels that conversation turns into a debate about whether the whole twin is real. With them, it is a line item.

A checklist I now use on day one

  • Pick the labels before collecting any data, and put them in the schema.
  • Make the build fail on a record with no source and no estimate flag.
  • Carry a simulated flag through every API and into every chart legend.
  • Draw built and designed parts differently in every diagram.
  • Write one page that lists what is real, what is not, and what would make it real.

None of this is sophisticated. It is the discipline a good plant already applies to its own data, applied to the twin. And it is the difference between a twin people use and one they politely admire.

entry.title: Write the contract first, what AI agents taught me about building fast
entry.summary: When several AI coding agents build one system in parallel, the speed comes from clear ownership and a written contract between the parts, not from the agents. The same lesson that makes human teams fast, learned again across three builds.
entry.content:
Over the last few weeks I have built several systems with AI coding agents working in parallel: a kitchen digital twin, a food bank twin built from a news video, and a research matchmaker that indexes 181,568 researchers. Each one was built by several agent threads at once, each owning one part of the repository.

The thing that decided how fast each build went was not the model, the prompt or the tooling. It was whether the parts had a written contract between them before anyone wrote code.

What goes wrong without one

Give several capable agents one goal and one repository, and they behave like several capable engineers in the same situation. Each makes reasonable local decisions. The 3D thread invents ids for the machines. The data thread invents different ones. The simulation thread reads a file shape that the data thread changes an hour later. Every part works on its own, and the system does not. The integration work at the end eats the time the parallelism saved.

What a contract looks like in practice

The contract does not need to be elaborate. In each build it was one or two things that every part agreed to read and write:

  • Kitchen twin: a set of ids (EQ-* for equipment, WC-* for work centers, RM-* for raw materials, FG-* for finished goods) and an ordered event log between the simulation and every view of it. The 3D scene places a model at each EQ-* id and exports a USD prim with the same name. The dashboard reports utilization by the same ids.
  • Food bank twin: OpenUSD in metres, Y up, with the floor at zero, plus a small JSON API in the same frame. The capture pipeline, the Blender model, the AWS backend and three different renderers never needed to know about each other.
  • Matchmaker: a published data format between the pipeline and the site, with versioned file formats (compact-v1, tags-v1) so the site can read old and new builds while the pipeline changes underneath it.

Ownership is the other half

Each thread owned a directory, and nobody edited anyone else's. When the simulation thread needed ingredient prices, it asked the data thread in a message, and the data thread added them. That sounds bureaucratic for software written in an afternoon. In practice it removed most merge conflicts and kept every change reviewable by the one thread that understood that part.

The kitchen twin's first version, fifteen pull requests across five threads, came together in a day because of that structure. Each pull request was built and tested by CI before merge, so the system was integrated continuously instead of at the end.

What still needs a person

Agents are very good at volume: sourcing and structuring data, writing an engine with tests, generating a 3D scene, keeping docs in step with code. The work that stayed with me was the work that does not parallelize:

  • Setting the bar. "Realistic", "private" and "no servers" had to be defined up front, in writing, before any thread started.
  • Choosing what is honest. Which numbers are labeled as estimates, what the demo is allowed to claim, and what the paper says about what failed.
  • Approving merges. CI catches breakage. Judgment about whether a change moves toward the goal is still a human call.

The takeaway

None of this is new. Interfaces before implementation, clear ownership and continuous integration are how good engineering teams have always moved fast. What is new is how much faster the cycle runs when the implementers are agents. A missing contract used to cost a week of integration. Now it can cost most of a one-day build. So write the contract first.
